message.content:
## Decision

Do not deploy this as designed. Node.js documentation explicitly states the Permission Model **cannot** be the sole tenant-isolation boundary for untrusted code. It is a "seat belt" that "does not provide security guarantees in the presence of malicious code" ([permissions.html#permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permissions)), and the security policy calls it a blast-radius reducer "not… a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process" ([SECURITY.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/node/v24.21.0/SECURITY.md)). Customer-uploaded JavaScript is exactly the trusted-code assumption this model rejects.

## Assumptions requiring change

- **`--permission-audit` in staging denies nothing.** It only publishes violations to diagnostics channels; execution continues ([#audit-mode](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#audit-mode)). It discovers required permissions; it is not a safety control.
- **`/srv/jobs/*.js` is far broader than intended.** "After passing a wildcard character (`*`) all subsequent characters will be ignored… `/home/*.js` will work similar to `/home/*`" ([#file-system-permissions](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#file-system-permissions)). This grants the whole `/srv/jobs` tree.
- **`--env-file` is not gated by the model.** Such flags read files before environment initialization and "are not subject to the rules of the Permission Model" ([#permission-model-constraints](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#permission-model-constraints)); its secrets reach the job via `process.env`.
- **Passing an already-open FD bypasses the model.** "Using existing file descriptors via the `node:fs` module bypasses the Permission Model" (same section).
- **Relative symlinks escape the grant.** "Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files… you must ensure that no paths to which access has been granted contain relative symbolic links" ([#limitations-and-known-issues](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v24.21.0/docs/api/permissions.html#limitations-and-known-issues)).
- Also relevant: `node:sqlite` and `process._debugProcess()` can reach resources with no grants (same pages).

## Worker inheritance — inconsistent

Sources conflict: permissions.html lists "The model does not inherit to a worker thread," while SECURITY.md says workers inherit the parent's restrictions and `execArgv` cannot expand them. **UNVERIFIED** — resolve against the v24 Node.js source/tests or a `worker_threads` issue before relying on it.

## Certification

No. These documents do not let you certify tenant isolation; use OS-level isolation (separate users, seccomp/AppArmor, containers). The model is useful only for trusted application code as defense-in-depth alongside `permission.drop()` and audit-mode discovery.

I have enough. Let me synthesize. Key points:

Facts:
1. Permission Model does not protect against malicious code (seat belt). From permissions.html intro. And SECURITY.md: "designed to reduce the blast radius of mistakes in trusted application code, not to act as a security boundary against intentional misuse or a compromised process." So using it as sole tenant-isolation boundary for untrusted customer JS is wrong premise.

2. --permission-audit: audit mode, does NOT deny; staging with audit means nothing is blocked. That's fine for discovery but not a safety control. Note audit mode added v24.20.0.

3. Literal argument /srv/jobs/*.js: "After passing a wildcard character (*) all subsequent characters will be ignored. For example: /home/*.js will work similar to /home/*." So /srv/jobs/*.js → effectively /srv/jobs/* — grants entire /srv/jobs directory. That's a broad grant. Also "When the permission model is initialized, it will automatically add a wildcard (*) if the specified directory exists."

4. --env-file outside the read list: "certain flags such as --env-file or --openssl-config are designed to read files before environment initialization. As a result, such flags are not subject to the rules of the Permission Model." So env-file file can be read regardless — meaning it's not an isolation bypass of the read list by the job, but the env vars (which may include secrets) become available to process.env, visible to the job. Actually with file descriptor... the point: --env-file reading is not gated. So it works but env vars are exposed to the untrusted job.

5. Already-open file descriptor: "Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model." So passing an open FD bypasses the FS permission — the job can read/write that FD regardless of read list. Big deal.

6. Symlinks: "Symbolic links will be followed even to locations outside of the set of paths that access has been granted to. Relative symbolic links may allow access to arbitrary files and directories. When starting applications with the permission model enabled, you must ensure that no paths to which access has been granted contain relative symbolic links." So relative symlinks in job dirs = escape. Must resolve with realpath / forbid symlinks.

7. --allow-worker: granted; conflicts about inheritance. permissions.html "Permission Model constraints": "The model does not inherit to a worker thread." But SECURITY.md: "Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process. Passing an empty or modified execArgv to a worker does not grant it additional permissions." And worker_threads.html: "Worker threads inherit non-process-specific options by default." These conflict. So the worker inheritance answer is UNVERIFIED/inconsistent. Must state limitation.

Actually let me be careful. The permissions.html "constraints" list explicitly says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread." The SECURITY.md says workers inherit the restrictions of their parent. These directly conflict for v24.21.0. So the proposal's assumption "workers inherit exactly the parent's restrictions" cannot be certified — evidence conflicts. Next evidence target: nodejs/node GitHub issues/PRs or the worker_threads permission implementation; or test files.

8. Also: node:sqlite — "It does not guarantee that users will not be able to access the file system through other means, such as through the node:sqlite module." So other modules can bypass.

9. process._debugProcess() callable with no grants — cross-process inspector activation. Same-OS-user risk.

10. Version: --permission-audit added in v24.20.0; v24.21.0 has it. Good. --allow-openssl-store added v24.21.0.

11. Security policy: threat model trusts the code it is asked to run; "The code run inherits all the privileges of the execution user." "Exposing Application-Level APIs to Untrusted Users (CWE-653)" — not Node.js vulnerabilities; app's responsibility to establish security boundaries. Also DoS: permission bypass not a vuln.

12. Bug bounty: "The Node.js project no longer has a bug bounty program." Minor.

Certification question: No — docs explicitly say it's not a security boundary for malicious code.

Useful for trusted code: seat belt to prevent accidental changes; audit mode for discovering needed permissions; permission.drop; config file; etc.
